Playtime–wellbeing associations are practically null across video game genres: a multi-platform digital trace registered report

Abstract

Video game research often treats games as a monolithic category, and single-game or single-platform studies leave open whether findings generalise across the medium. In this registered report, we used multi-platform digital trace data from the Open Play dataset to test whether (H1) total playtime is meaningfully associated with mental wellbeing and (H2) whether this association differs by game genre. The data comprise 226,000 hours of playtime telemetry across 4,154 titles from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam for 1,838 UK and US adults, linked to structured genre metadata and to 6,680 biweekly mental wellbeing assessments (SWEMWBS). Bayesian multilevel within-between models evaluated both hypotheses against a pre-registered threshold for practical significance. Total playtime was practically equivalent to zero on both dimensions: wellbeing barely moved in waves when participants played more than their own average, and those who habitually played more reported slightly lower wellbeing, well under the threshold of practical significance. Contrary to our registered prediction that genres would differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in mental wellbeing, genre differences fell below the threshold across three model specifications, including a multi-membership model for games carrying multiple genre labels. Genres proved statistically distinguishable but practically interchangeable. A further exploratory analysis extended these tests to the daily timescale and found the same result, namely a small positive within-person trend far below practical significance and a between-person contrast leaning negative within the equivalence region. The playtime–wellbeing null thus survives its strictest test to date and generalises across genres, with slight heterogeneity detected and bounded below any practically meaningful magnitude. Genre differences appear to be the wrong place to look for gaming’s wellbeing effects; genre labels are too coarse a proxy for the psychological experiences that plausibly drive them, which directs attention towards finer-grained characterisations of play.

Introduction

Video game effects research utilising digital trace data often focuses on a single game or a handful of games to understand the psychological processes and outcomes of digital play (Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025; Brühlmann et al., 2020; Johannes et al., 2021; Larrieu et al., 2023). While understandable given the limited resources and lack of objective data available to independent researchers, it has left the field guessing whether identified relationships are unique to the studied titles or whether they apply universally across games. This limitation has restricted researchers’ abilities to estimate the true prevalence of any found effects, leading to assumptions of generalisability and the formation of theories that fail to capture the diversity of the medium. Potential overgeneralisation of findings has been well-documented in psychological research and is particularly pertinent to research on video games (Yarkoni, 2019).

With more than 10,000 new games released each year (Notis, 2021), an accessible classification system is essential for studying and comparing video games at scale. Genres, while defined by convention and neither exclusive nor exhaustive as labels (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025; Clarke et al., 2017; Vargas-Iglesias, 2020), remain the most pragmatic means of categorising video games, providing utility for researchers, players, industry, and policymakers alike. Psychologists have been trying to classify game genres for decades (Griffiths, 1993; Wolf, 2002), but must negotiate challenges in definition, overlaps between genres, and the continuous evolution of genres as new games are released. Genres are therefore best treated not as definitive taxonomical statements but as crude yet practical tools for organising a growing and diversifying library.

Studies have documented marked differences between video game genres in terms of their playtime and their effects on player behaviour, cognition, and wellbeing (André et al., 2024; Dobrowolski et al., 2015; Hazel et al., 2022; Raith et al., 2021). Action games have been linked to increased visual attention (Palaus et al., 2017), cognitive and attentional control (Anguera et al., 2013; Bavelier & Green, 2019), and working memory (Blacker et al., 2014). Massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs), first-person shooters, real-time strategy games (RTS), and Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games have been associated with higher gaming disorder (GD) symptoms (Elliott et al., 2012; Rehbein et al., 2021). At the same time, randomised controlled trials have employed genres like casual games and exergames to induce positive moods and reduce stress (Huang et al., 2017; Russoniello et al., 2009). These findings suggest that the effects of video games are not uniform and that genre helps shape both gaming behaviour and its impact on wellbeing.

A recent systematic review, however, documented inconsistencies in how genres are classified across psychological research (Starosta et al., 2024). Of 96 examined articles, only 50 (52%) employed an existing genre classification; 46 (48%) used a unique classification, and 18 (19%) failed to specify the basis or definitions of their genre categorisations altogether. Genre classifications were typically self-reported by participants or assigned by authors, and the same games are habitually classified into different genres across studies. This subjectivity undermines the validity of existing self-report or researcher-ascribed genre taxonomies.

Structured, crowd-sourced metadata repositories such as SteamDB, The Games Database, and the Internet Games Database (IGDB) offer a more reliable alternative, involving both game developers and large player samples in collaboratively maintaining genre labels (Lee et al., 2015; Li & Zhang, 2020; Starosta et al., 2024). This approach accommodates the fluidity of genres over time (Cohen, 1986) and enables comparative research at scale. Yet several methodological obstacles have prevented genre-level research using digital trace data. Data access is fragmented: digital trace data are siloed within individual platform holders, and no cross-platform standard exists for recording or sharing gameplay telemetry (Zendle et al., 2023). The choice of taxonomy is also not neutral: genre labels conflate distinct facets of games, such as gameplay style, purpose, and mood (Lee et al., 2014); treating players as pure-genre versus acknowledging multi-genre play alters conclusions about player characteristics (Azizi et al., 2018), and factor-analytic decompositions of crowd-sourced game tags produce genre structures that diverge from conventional labels (Li, 2020).

The Present Study

In sum, one portion of the literature has shown that playtime undifferentiated by genre is not a meaningful predictor of wellbeing, using data from both specific games (Larrieu et al., 2023) and platforms (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024; Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025). This relationship, however, has not yet been tested using comprehensive multi-platform play data. Furthermore, multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain why aggregate playtime is poorly predictive of wellbeing, including displacement of beneficial activities, satisfaction or frustration of basic psychological needs, and selection effects whereby individuals with lower wellbeing play more (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025). Most proposed mechanisms operate at the level of game features or player experience rather than at the level of total time spent; playtime is, at best, a moderator (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025). The only causal evidence to date, exploiting console lotteries as a natural experiment, found positive effects of gaming on wellbeing, with heterogeneous effects by console type (Egami et al., 2024), suggesting that observational null findings may reflect confounding rather than absence of effect. Thus, our first hypothesis predicts the absence of a meaningful relationship, this time with digital trace data across several platforms and thousands of games:

H1. Total cross-platform playtime is not meaningfully associated with fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (H1a, “within-person”) or with average wellbeing over the full study period (H1b, “between-person”).

We test this via a Bayesian ROPE analysis with equivalence bounds of ±0.06 SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day, matching the SESOI used by Ballou, Sewall, et al. (2024). In practical terms, H1a asks whether playing more than one’s own average in a given two-week wave is associated with a shift in wellbeing, while H1b asks whether individuals who habitually play more report different average wellbeing than those who play less. The within-person component isolates the effect of playtime fluctuations from stable individual differences; the between-person component captures the cross-sectional association, which is inherently more vulnerable to confounding by self-selection.

Consistent null findings for the effects of playtime on wellbeing have generated calls for the unpacking of raw decontextualised playtime into more informative measures that consider games’ varied characteristics and affordances (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024). Game genres offer a structured way to differentiate between video games and their corresponding play experiences (Starosta et al., 2024). While genre differences are widely established (Azizi et al., 2018; Dobrowolski et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2016; Rehbein et al., 2021), the effects of genre-level playtime on wellbeing are yet to be studied using digital trace data. Following previous literature, we predict that genres vary in their relation to wellbeing, with some potentially positive and others potentially negative, varying in strength. Put more formally:

H2. Genres differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing over a 2-week period (H2a, “within-person”) and to average wellbeing over the full study period (H2b, “between-person”).

H2a asks: when a participant plays more than their own average this wave, does it matter what genres that extra playtime is in? H2b asks the between-person complement: among people who play more overall, does it matter whether that habitual extra playtime is concentrated in RPGs versus Shooters versus other genres? If H2 is supported, and genre-specific associations differ from one another, it would provide a candidate explanation for the consistent null aggregate findings: undifferentiated playtime measures may average over heterogeneous genre effects that cancel in aggregate. H2 thus tests whether it is justified to generalise video game effects across genres, testing the generalisability that single-title studies must assume (Yarkoni, 2019). Taken together, the two hypotheses form a single generalisability test rather than two separate null results: H1 establishes whether an aggregate association exists, and H2 establishes whether that aggregate conceals genre-level associations that offset one another. The generalisability critique is widely cited but has yet to be operationalised as a quantity a study can estimate.

Beyond the registered hypotheses, we report one unregistered extension. The biweekly window aggregates many individual play sessions into a single retrospective judgement, so the registered tests leave open whether associations operating on shorter timescales are hidden by aggregation. As such, we re-examine both hypotheses at the daily level. This extension was specified after the registered analyses were complete and is reported as exploratory throughout (see Exploratory Daily-Timescale Analysis in Methods).

Methods

Data Source and Participants

The analyses reported here are part of a Stage 1 Registered Report (Ballou, Földes, et al., 2024), and the data collected for this study are part of the Open Play dataset (Ballou, Földes, et al., 2025), a longitudinal dataset that combined multi-platform video game digital trace data alongside daily and biweekly psychological measures from adult gamers in the UK and US over a three-month period. The intake surveys were completed between Sep 2024 and Jan 2026. Digital trace data span the following periods: Nintendo (May 2022 to Oct 2025), Xbox (May 2022 to Sep 2025), Steam (Nov 2024 to Oct 2025), iOS (Mar 2025 to Aug 2025), Android (Mar 2025 to Aug 2025).

This study received ethical approval from the Social Sciences and Humanities Inter-Divisional Research Ethics Committee at the University of Oxford (OII_CIA_23_107). All participants provided informed consent at the start of the study, including consent to their data being shared openly for reanalysis.

Participants were paid at an average rate of £12/hour, equating to: £0.20 for a 1-minute screening, £2 for the 10-minute intake survey (plus £5 for linking at least one account with recent data), £0.80 for each 4-minute daily survey, and £2 for each 10-minute biweekly survey. Participants received a £10 bonus payment for completing at least 24 out of 30 daily surveys and/or 5 out of 6 biweekly surveys.

From 35,369 participants who completed the intake survey, 2,544 met the pre-registered screening and linking criteria. The analytic sample comprises the 1,838 participants who provided valid SWEMWBS responses in at least one biweekly survey wave. Playtime for these participants is measured from their linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam accounts; participants and waves without recorded play on these platforms contribute zero hours, and 1,541 participants (84%) had at least one gameplay session of a game that could be matched to a genre. The demographic sensitivity analysis uses the 1,741 participants with a matching qualified intake record and age within the 18–40 screening range (1,041 US, 700 UK; mean age 26.9 years, 66% men); 97 analytic-sample participants are excluded from that subset (97 without a matching intake record, 0 aged over 40). Full demographic characteristics, including country-level breakdowns, are reported in Table 3.

Measures

The distributions and structure of the key variables are visualised in Figure 2.

Wellbeing. Wellbeing was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale [SWEMWBS; Tennant et al. (2007)], a 7-item short form of the WEMWBS covering psychological functioning and subjective wellbeing over the past 2 weeks, with responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from “None of the time” to “All of the time.” Scores are computed as the arithmetic mean of the 7 items (range: 1–5). All reported coefficients, priors, and the pre-registered SESOI are defined on this item-mean scale.

Video game playtime. Digital trace data from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam provide session-level records (per-title start and end timestamps), while iOS and Android contribute only daily aggregate minutes (no game-level metadata). Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam therefore contribute to both H1 (total playtime) and H2 (genre-specific playtime); iOS and Android contribute only to the pre-registered all-platform sensitivity analysis (Appendix B, Deviation D6). Total playtime is computed from raw sessions without multi-genre duplication (see Multi-genre attribution below).

Game genre classification. Game genre labels for Nintendo and Steam are obtained by cross-referencing game titles in the digital trace data with the Internet Games Database (IGDB). IGDB is, to our knowledge, the only database with complete multi-platform metadata coverage that offers an API for programmatic data retrieval. The genre labels are crowd-sourced: community members can submit contributions (e.g., a new game or alternative categorisation), which are vetted by admins and moderators before appearing in the database. For Xbox, game titles could not be matched to IGDB genre labels, since Xbox provided us only with anonymised title identifiers. Still, genre labels were available through the Xbox store and were mapped onto the IGDB taxonomy. A string-formatting issue in the upstream mapping pipeline had left approximately 67% of Xbox playtime unmapped; we corrected this locally using the xbox_primary_genre and xbox_subgenre metadata fields, increasing Xbox genre coverage from 33% to 80% of playtime (see Appendix B, Deviation U1). In total, we collected 23 distinct raw IGDB genre labels and collapsed them into 14 study-level categories (e.g., Strategy subsumes Turn-Based Strategy (TBS), Real-Time Strategy (RTS), Tactical, and MOBA; Puzzle subsumes Card & Board Game and Quiz/Trivia). The complete mapping table can be found in Appendix A, and the descriptive statistics by genre in Appendix C. We did not consider IGDB “themes” or other metadata fields. Overall, 94.1% of in-study playtime is matched to at least one study genre (Steam 96.3%, Nintendo 92.3%, Xbox 80.2%); unmatched playtime counts towards total playtime but towards no genre.

Genre co-occurrence and compositional multi-genre attribution. Nowadays, games rarely carry just one genre. Across the 3,721 individual games in our dataset, 62% carry more than one genre label, leading to 325 distinct genre combinations. Figure 1 shows the playtime-weighted co-occurrence structure across the 40 most-played combinations, and Table 1 lists the fifteen most-played combinations with their top titles. Operationalising games as multi-genre has consequential effects in relation to playtime. Namely, instead of treating genre as a partition of time (which only works for single-genre games), we more accurately treat genre as a weighted compositional exposure to that genre’s play: a 60-minute session of an Adventure-RPG (e.g., Skyrim) therefore contributes equal weight (i.e., 1) to the Adventure exposure and to the RPG exposure. In the absence of genre weights, partitioning the 60-minute session between the two genres is not only arbitrary (is it 20 minutes of Adventure and 40 minutes of RPG?), it would also understate exposure compared to single-genre games. For example, if that person also played 60 minutes of a single-genre RPG (e.g., Final Fantasy XIV Online), the total compositional exposure under a partial attribution of assumed equal weights (30 minutes of Adventure and 30 minutes of RPG for Skyrim, and 60 minutes of RPG for Final Fantasy XIV Online) would be 0.5 hours of Adventure and 1.5 hours of RPG, which looks like the person played three times as much RPG as Adventure. The genre exposure weights under the full attribution would be 1 hour for Adventure and 2 hours for RPG, indicating double the RPG exposure compared to Adventure, which reflects the play more accurately than the partial attribution.

Since the playtime of our participants consists of many different multi-genre games played over prolonged periods of time, we operationalise genre exposure as compositional and use full attribution to calculate the genre-exposure weights (see Appendix B, Deviation D1; the pre-registered primary-genre analysis is reported in supplementary materials). As such, each genre coefficient estimates the association between exposure to games carrying that genre and wellbeing.

Demographics. Age, gender, ethnicity, country, and employment were collected at baseline via self-report. Full demographic characteristics are reported in Table 3 in Appendix C.

Analytic Approach

All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2025), and the manuscript was written in Quarto (Allaire et al., 2025). We fit four Bayesian multilevel models with brms (Bürkner, 2017). H1 is addressed by a random-effects within-between (REWB) regression (M0) and by a Bayesian multi-membership model (M3); H2 is addressed by a fixed-effects model (M1), a hierarchical prior model (M2), and the multi-membership model (M3). The three genre models differ in how much information the estimate for one genre shares with the estimates for the others: M1 estimates each genre’s coefficients independently (the pre-registered structure), M2 places a common prior distribution over the genre coefficients and estimates its standard deviation (partial pooling), and M3 assigns each wave to the genres it contains in proportion to their playtime shares (multi-membership). Deviations from the pre-registered plan are catalogued in Appendix B and are flagged below where they affect interpretation.

All models use a within-between decomposition of playtime: the between-person component is defined as the participant’s average across the study, and the within-person component as the deviation of a given wave from that personal average. The two components answer different questions. The within-person coefficient describes whether a participant’s wellbeing changes in waves in which they play more than they usually do, because each participant serves as their own comparison. The between-person coefficient describes whether participants who habitually play more report different average wellbeing than participants who habitually play less; this comparison is made across people.

M0: Total Playtime

M0 addresses H1: is total playtime across Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam associated with wellbeing? The model is a random-effects within-between (REWB) regression and returns the two coefficients, \beta_W for within-person fluctuations and \beta_B for habitual between-person differences. Each participant receives a random intercept, because people differ in baseline wellbeing, and a random slope for within-person playtime, because the association need not be identical for everyone. Priors are calibrated to the 1–5 outcome scale. The intercept prior is centred on the scale midpoint, and the coefficient priors are weakly informative, leaving effects up to roughly 1 point per hour/day plausible while regularising implausibly large values.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \beta_W \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + \beta_B \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} \\ \begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right) \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\ \beta_W, \beta_B &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5) \end{aligned}

M1: Fixed-Effects

M1 is the pre-registered specification for H2. Each of the 14 genres receives its own within-person and between-person coefficient, estimated independently, with a random intercept per participant. Independent estimation has a benefit and a cost. The benefit is that the model imposes no assumptions about how similar genres are to one another. The cost is that rarely played genres are estimated from little data and therefore receive wide credible intervals, which is the problem that M2 and M3 address. Because genre exposures are non-exclusive, they cannot be summed to recover total playtime, and M1 therefore contains no separate total-playtime term. Two departures from the registered specification should be noted: exposures use full attribution rather than primary-genre labels (Deviation D1), and the registered random slopes for all genre terms (28 additional parameters) proved near-singular, so we followed the pre-registered contingency plan and retained the random intercept only.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) + u_{0j} \\ u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{pid}}) \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\ \beta_{W,g}, \beta_{B,g} &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5) \end{aligned}

M2: Hierarchical Prior

M2 keeps M1’s structure but changes how the genre coefficients are estimated, and this change yields a direct answer to H2. Rather than treating the 14 coefficients as unrelated, M2 assumes that they are drawn from a common normal distribution centred at zero and estimates the standard deviation of that distribution, τgenre, separately for the within-person and between-person dimensions. τgenre is therefore an estimate of exactly the quantity H2 asks about: how much the genre coefficients differ from one another, expressed in outcome units per hour of play. The shared distribution also produces partial pooling. Estimates for rarely played genres are pulled towards the common centre, whereas genres with ample data retain estimates close to their independent values.

The Half-Normal(0, 0.1) hyperprior on τ is matched to the outcome scale. Genre coefficients are expressed in SWEMWBS points per hour/day, and the smallest effect size of interest is 0.06 on that scale, so a much wider hyperprior would place substantial prior mass on heterogeneity far larger than any effect considered plausible. The sensitivity of the results to halving and doubling this scale is examined in Appendix D. Sampling near τ = 0 is numerically difficult, so we use conservative sampler settings and report divergence counts and R-hat diagnostics for every model alongside the results.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \sum_{g=1}^{G}\bigl(\beta_{W,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{within},g,ij} + \beta_{B,g}\, \text{Time}_{\text{between},g,j}\bigr) + u_{0j} \\ u_{0j} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{pid}}) \\ \beta_{W,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{within}}) \\ \beta_{B,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau_{\text{between}}) \\ \tau_{\text{within}}, \tau_{\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Normal}(0, 0.1) \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \end{aligned}

M3: Multi-Membership

M3 represents each wave the way panel D of Figure 2 displays it, namely as a total amount of playtime with a genre composition. The model retains total playtime as the predictor, inheriting M0’s structure including the overall \beta_W and \beta_B, and allows the composition of that playtime to modify the playtime slope. Formally, this is a multi-membership structure, where each wave carries all 14 genre labels and only the weights vary, equal to each genre’s share of exposure. As such, a wave consisting mostly of Shooter play is governed mostly by the Shooter slope adjustment, and a wave divided between Adventure and RPG draws on both adjustments in proportion.

Each genre’s slope adjustment is drawn from a common distribution, and the standard deviation of that distribution, σs, is this model’s answer to H2: it quantifies how much the playtime–wellbeing slope varies with the genres being played.

\begin{aligned} \text{SWEMWBS}_{ij} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma) \\ \mu_{ij} &= \alpha + \beta_W \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + \beta_B \text{Time}_{\text{between},j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} \\ &\quad + \sum_{g=1}^{G} w_{g,ij}(s_{W,g} \text{Time}_{\text{within},ij} + s_{B,g} \text{Time}_{\text{between},j}) \\ \begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{Normal}\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\right) \\ s_{W,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_s) \\ s_{B,g} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_{s,\text{between}}) \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 3, 2) \\ \beta_W, \beta_B &\sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 0.5) \\ \sigma_s, \sigma_{s,\text{between}} &\sim \text{Half-Normal}(0, 0.3) \end{aligned}

Because this use of multi-membership is unconventional, we validated the specification by parameter recovery before fitting it to real data. Synthetic datasets with known genre-slope heterogeneity were fit with identical model code; every population-level parameter, including σs, was recovered within its 95% credible interval, with no divergent transitions (simulation report in the supplementary materials).

Missing Data

Missingness in the outcome takes two forms. Item-level missingness is rare and all-or-nothing: 43 submitted surveys lack SWEMWBS, each missing all seven items. Wave nonresponse is the dominant form: survey completion declined from 100% at wave 1 to 40% at wave 6, leaving 4,348 of the 11,028 analytic person-waves (39.4%) without an observed SWEMWBS. Playtime was not imputed: tracking was continuous and automatic, so within linked platforms an absence of play is recorded absence rather than missing data, and exposures exist for every person-wave.

The primary Bayesian models are fit to the observed outcomes; this is valid provided outcome missingness is at random given the modelled covariates and random effects. To test that assumption, we multiply imputed SWEMWBS on the complete participant × wave grid, using the two-level protocol shared with the programmatic registered report’s sibling Stage 2 studies: multiple imputation by chained equations [mice and miceadds; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn (2011); Robitzsch & Grund (2024)] with predictive mean matching (2l.pmm), participants as random-intercept clusters (van Buuren, 2018), and m = 100 imputations set from the pilot fraction of missing information by von Hippel’s (2020) two-stage rule. Predictive mean matching donates observed values, so imputed scores respect the 1–5 scale. Frequentist counterparts of the analysis models were fit to each imputed dataset and pooled by Rubin’s rules; the pooled results do not meaningfully differ from the complete-case analyses (Appendix D, Table 8).

Smallest Effect Size of Interest

Establishing the absence of a practically significant effect requires committing in advance to a threshold below which an association is too small to matter, the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI). By practically significant, we mean the smallest change in wellbeing that a player would themselves notice, known also as a minimally important difference (MID). Following previous studies, the MID is set at 0.3 points on the 1–5 SWEMWBS scale, converging with anchor-based estimates of the WEMWBS [Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale; Ballou, Sewall, et al. (2024); Maheswaran et al. (2012)] and the PANAS [Positive and Negative Affect Schedule; Anvari & Lakens (2021)].

To calculate the SESOI, we also need to know how large a change in playtime is realistically available to reach the MID. Because UK and US adults average approximately 5 hours of daily leisure time (Sturm & Cohen, 2019), this provides us with an upper bound on how much daily play could plausibly rise or fall without it displacing other behaviours that arguably impact wellbeing more than play (e.g., sleep). SESOI is the ratio of the two: 0.3 ÷ 5 = 0.06 points per hour. An association smaller than this means that even a person who shifted their entire 5-hour daily leisure time budget into or out of gaming would not experience a noticeable change in wellbeing.

We evaluate all coefficients against the interval between the negative and positive SESOI [−0.06, +0.06], also known as the Region of Practical Equivalence [ROPE; Kruschke (2018)]. If a coefficient’s 95% credible interval (CrI) falls entirely inside the ROPE, the effect is considered practically null, meaning even the largest plausible effect is too small to matter; entirely above +0.06, practically positive; entirely below −0.06, practically negative. A CrI straddling either edge of the ROPE is inconclusive.

Exploratory Daily-Timescale Analysis

To assess whether our findings hold on a shorter timescale, we conducted an exploratory daily-timescale analysis. The daily extension is unregistered; an analysis plan fixed the exposure window, sample criteria, model set, priors, and SESOI before any exposure–outcome model was estimated. US participants were asked to complete daily surveys for the first 30 study days, including a life-satisfaction item (“I was satisfied with my life today”) answered on a 0–100 slider (Ballou, Földes, et al., 2025), which serves as the outcome. Exposure is console and PC playtime from 4:00 a.m. local time of the response’s waking day up to the survey completion timestamp, computed from the same session-level telemetry and full-attribution genre assignment as the main analysis, with local time taken from each participant’s reported timezone; Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps (8% of sessions) have their minutes spread uniformly over the recorded day. Of 15.8K diary responses from 1.2K participants, 13.0K responses (82.6%) from 763 participants had available telemetry and analysable same-day windows; exclusions were dominated by days without telemetry coverage. Excluded responses enter an all-responses sensitivity refit that retains every response and scores unobserved play as zero.

The within-between decomposition is hybrid: within-person terms are deviations from a person’s own same-day average, and between-person terms are habitual full-day hours (a participant’s total telemetry over their observed diary period divided by days), which keeps habitual contrasts in daily-hour units directly comparable with the registered analysis. Because the pre-registered SESOI is defined on the SWEMWBS item-mean scale, a SESOI for the slider is constructed the same way, dividing a minimally important difference by the roughly five hours of daily leisure realistically available (Sturm & Cohen, 2019). We adopt a minimally important difference of 5 slider points, below both a distribution-based half within-person standard deviation (6.3 points) and the registered minimally important difference expressed as a share of its scale range (7.5%, or 7.5 slider points); the daily SESOI is therefore 1 slider point per hour of daily play, a deliberately conservative choice, since a smaller minimally important difference makes practical equivalence harder to claim rather than easier. The model specifications (M0–M3) are refit at the daily level. Robustness refits (autocorrelated residuals with a day trend, adjustment for window length, exclusion of the date-only Xbox sessions, and the all-responses sample) are reported in Appendix D.

Results

Our analytic sample comprised 1,838 participants with valid SWEMWBS responses in at least one biweekly wave, yielding 6,680 person-wave observations (M = 3.6 of 6 waves per participant; survey response declined from 100% at wave 1 to 40% at wave 6, see Missing Data and Appendix D). Playtime is measured from linked Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam telemetry, with zero hours recorded for participants and waves without play on these platforms. Participants played an average of 1.67 hours per day (SD = 2) on Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam combined. The most played genres were Role Playing Game (RPG) and Adventure.

Data Quality Controls

Prior to hypothesis testing, we conducted the three pre-registered positive data quality controls (DQCs) to validate expected patterns in the data. First, self-reported biweekly playtime correlated positively with digital trace playtime (r = 0.469, one-sided 95% lower bound = 0.451, p < .001). Second, session integrity largely held. Xbox contained 0 overlapping sessions, and no Steam session’s recorded playtime exceeded its elapsed wall-clock duration (0 violations). Nintendo retained a small number of overlapping sessions: 675 of 288,082 sessions (0.23%), with a median overlap of 9.8 minutes and accounting for 0.09% of total Nintendo playtime. These pairs reflect concurrent use of multiple consoles linked to one account: 529 of the 675 pairs involved two different games recorded as running at once, and 95 involved two distinct console models (e.g., a Switch Lite overlapping an OLED model), which requires two physical devices; because the device identifier records the model rather than the individual console, some same-model pairs likely also reflect two consoles. The overlaps were also concentrated in a few accounts, with two participants alone contributing 236 pairs. Given their rarity and their small share of playtime, we judged these overlaps too small to materially influence the wave-level aggregates. Third, men played more shooter games than women (M = 0.487 vs. 0.309 hrs/day, t(1144.4) = 4.25, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.21), meeting the pre-registered criterion of a significant difference in the expected direction and consistent with population studies of gendered genre preferences (Rehbein et al., 2016). We therefore proceeded with the confirmatory analyses.

Code 
h1_model <- brm(
  bf(wemwbs ~ total_within + total_between +
       (1 + total_within | pid)),
  data    = analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  # Priors rescaled for the 1-5 outcome scale (wemwbs is rowMeans on 1-5).
  # Intercept centred at 3 (midpoint of 1-5); coefficient scale tightened
  # from 2.5 to 0.5 to be weakly informative on the 1-5 outcome range.
  prior   = prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "b") +
            prior(student_t(3, 3, 2),   class = "Intercept"),
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h1_rewb_model")
)
Code 
h2_formula <- bf(paste(
  "wemwbs ~",
  paste(c(gh_within, gh_between), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (1 | pid)"
))

h2_model <- brm(
  formula = h2_formula,
  data    = analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  # Priors rescaled for the 1-5 outcome scale (see H1 comment).
  prior   = prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "b") +
            prior(student_t(3, 3, 2),   class = "Intercept"),
  family  = gaussian(),
  chains  = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 8675309,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file    = here("models/h2_genre_model")
)
Code 
# Two learned hyperparameters: tau_genre_within (H2a) and tau_genre_between (H2b).
# Each genre's within-person coefficient is drawn from Normal(0, tau_within);
# each genre's between-person coefficient from Normal(0, tau_between).
# Both receive Half-Normal(0, 0.1) hyperpriors scaled for the 1-5 outcome.
sv_hier <- stanvar(
  scode = "real<lower=0> tau_genre_within;\nreal<lower=0> tau_genre_between;",
  block = "parameters"
) +
stanvar(
  scode = paste(
    "target += normal_lpdf(tau_genre_within | 0, 0.1) - normal_lccdf(0 | 0, 0.1);",
    "target += normal_lpdf(tau_genre_between | 0, 0.1) - normal_lccdf(0 | 0, 0.1);",
    sep = "\n"
  ),
  block = "model"
)

# Hierarchical priors on BOTH within and between genre coefficients
hier_priors_within <- do.call(c, lapply(gh_within, function(g) {
  set_prior("normal(0, tau_genre_within)", class = "b", coef = g)
}))
hier_priors_between <- do.call(c, lapply(gh_between, function(g) {
  set_prior("normal(0, tau_genre_between)", class = "b", coef = g)
}))

h2_hier_priors <- c(
  # Default weakly informative prior for any genre coefficients not covered
  # by the explicit hierarchical priors below
  set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 0.5)", class = "b"),
  set_prior("student_t(3, 3, 2)",   class = "Intercept"),
  hier_priors_within,
  hier_priors_between
)

# Same genre-exposure structure as M1, but with hierarchical priors on
# genre coefficients. No total_within/total_between: genre exposure columns
# are non-exclusive (full attribution), so partialing out total playtime
# would leave only multi-genre inflation artifacts.
h2_hier_formula <- bf(paste(
  "wemwbs ~",
  paste(c(gh_within, gh_between), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (1 | pid)"
))

h2_hier_model <- brm(
  formula  = h2_hier_formula,
  data     = analysis_data |> filter(!is.na(wemwbs)),
  prior    = h2_hier_priors,
  stanvars = sv_hier,
  family   = gaussian(),
  chains   = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000, seed = 2025,
  control  = list(adapt_delta = 0.999, max_treedepth = 15),
  file     = here("models/h2_hier_model_v2")
)

H1: Total Playtime and Wellbeing

Figure 3 summarises the H1 results; the underlying posterior summaries for all hypothesis tests are tabulated in Appendix E (Table 10). For the within-person effect (H1a), the posterior mean was 0.003 SWEMWBS item-mean points per hour/day (95% CrI: [-0.008, 0.014]), with 100% of the posterior inside the ROPE, above the 95% posterior-mass criterion. Therefore, when a participant plays more than their own average in a given wave, their wellbeing does not change to any practically meaningful degree, supporting H1a. For the between-person effect (H1b), the posterior mean was -0.017 (95% CrI: [-0.035, 0.001]), with 100% of the posterior inside the ROPE, likewise establishing practical equivalence. The between-person estimate leans negative (its credible interval extends just to zero), but its magnitude is far below the SESOI: even a 2 hour/day difference in habitual playtime would correspond to only -0.034 points on the 1–5 scale (about 0.8% of the 4-point range).

Both components of H1 are therefore supported. The model also bounds person-to-person variation in the within-person association: the random-slope SD was 0.035 (95% CrI: [0.005, 0.062]), with 3.8% of its posterior above the SESOI.

The multi-membership model also provides H1 estimates via its fixed effects. Figure 3 confirms that M0 and M3 yield consistent H1 estimates, and that the inclusion of genre-level terms in M3 does not alter the overall playtime–wellbeing association.

H2: Genre-Specific Effects

H2 asks whether genres differ in how playtime relates to wellbeing. We answer it in two steps. First, we report the genre heterogeneity parameters, which provide a direct test of H2: how much do genre-specific playtime slopes vary? Second, we examine the per-genre estimates the three specifications produce. A further exploratory analysis asks whether these effects hold at the daily level.

Genre Heterogeneity

Figure 4 shows the posterior distributions for the genre heterogeneity statistics from all three H2 models. M1’s statistic is the standard deviation of the 14 independent within-person genre coefficients; M2’s is τgenre from the learned hierarchical prior; M3’s is σs from the multi-membership random effects. All three are in the same units (SWEMWBS item-mean per hour/day) and represent how much genre-specific playtime slopes vary across genres.

The primary test of H2 comes from the multi-membership model’s (M3) genre heterogeneity parameters. For the within-person dimension (H2a), the posterior mean of \sigma_{s,\text{within}} was 0.044 (95% CrI: [0.006, 0.1]). Because a standard deviation cannot be negative, the ROPE is the SESOI of 0.06, which is exceeded by 21.9% of the posterior. The data are thus most consistent with genre-to-genre variation in within-person slopes that is smaller than the smallest effect of interest, though the wide interval means heterogeneity of up to roughly 0.1 points per hour/day cannot be ruled out. For the between-person dimension (H2b), \sigma_{s,\text{between}} = 0.017 (95% CrI: [0.001, 0.046]), with only 0.5% of the posterior exceeding the SESOI, meaning that between-person genre heterogeneity is practically negligible.

Genre variation in within-person slopes (H2a) is practically negligible under the hierarchical prior model (M2): τwithin = 0.014 (95% CrI: [0.004, 0.028]), with 100% of the posterior inside the ROPE (±0.06). The results are the same for the between-person dimension (H2b), τbetween = 0.021 (95% CrI: [0.004, 0.05]), with 99.2% of the posterior inside the ROPE, showing that individuals who habitually favour certain genres do not meaningfully differ in average wellbeing from those who favour others.

Finally, the pre-registered fixed-effects specification (M1) provides the simplest version of the test. We computed the standard deviation of the 14 genre-specific within-person coefficients at each posterior draw: every iteration of the Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler yields one full set of the 14 coefficients, and therefore one SD, so the spread across genres is itself estimated with uncertainty attached. The posterior mean of this heterogeneity SD was 0.032 (95% CrI: [0.02, 0.047]), an interval that lies entirely below the SESOI of 0.06. For between-person effects the heterogeneity SD was 0.076 (95% CrI: [0.044, 0.123]), the only statistic among the three specifications to exceed the SESOI; as discussed below, this raw SD includes sampling error and should be read as an upper bound.

The H2 heterogeneity estimates converge on a consistent qualitative picture: genre-to-genre variation in per-hour wellbeing slopes is practically negligible and at most small. On the within-person dimension, M2’s τ (0.014) and M1’s raw SD (0.032) both fall entirely below 0.06, while M3’s σs (0.044) straddles the boundary with about a fifth of its posterior above it. On the between-person dimension, the two pooled estimates (M2, M3) fall below the SESOI while M1’s raw SD exceeds it. M1’s SD is the empirical standard deviation of 14 independently estimated coefficients and therefore includes estimation error, especially from rare genres with wide posteriors; M2’s τ and M3’s σs are model-estimated pooling parameters that separate signal from noise. Overall, the pooled specifications place genre heterogeneity below the pre-registered equivalence threshold on both dimensions, and no specification provides positive evidence of practically meaningful genre differences.

The heterogeneity estimates and convergence diagnostics for all three specifications are tabulated in Appendix E (Table 10). Full posterior summaries for all four models are provided in the supplementary materials.

Per-Genre Estimates

Figure 5 shows the per-genre exposure coefficients from the three H2 specifications, with the within-person and between-person dimensions in side-by-side panels; each genre row shows M1 (circle), M2 (square), and M3 (diamond). We describe each model’s estimates in turn before comparing them.

Under the fixed-effects specification (M1), the 14 within-person point estimates cluster near zero, and 8 of the 14 credible intervals fall entirely inside the ROPE; the remainder straddle a boundary rather than exclude it. The cost of independent estimation is visible in the interval widths: the widest within-person interval (Point-and-Click) is roughly 5 times wider than the narrowest, too wide to support any genre-specific conclusion for rarely played genres. Between persons the intervals are wider still, with 2 of the 14 entirely inside the ROPE.

The hierarchical prior model (M2) pulls these estimates towards their common centre: 14 of the 14 within-person genre coefficients have 95% CrIs that fall entirely within the pre-registered ROPE band (±0.06). The between-person coefficients are wider but show a similar pattern, with Sport as the genre whose point estimate sits closest to the upper ROPE boundary.

The multi-membership model (M3) estimates each genre as a deviation from the overall playtime slope; with the overall fixed effect added back, its within-person estimates span -0.023 to 0.048 and its between-person estimates -0.033 to -0.006, with 1 and 12 of the 14 intervals respectively falling entirely inside the ROPE.

The three model specifications thus converge on a consistent per-genre pattern for both within- and between-person effects. The primary visible difference is that M2 and M3 produce narrower credible intervals for rare genres (Visual Novel, Fighting, Point-and-Click) relative to M1’s wider independent estimates, reflecting the partial pooling that each achieves through different mechanisms. For common genres, the three specifications produce near-identical point estimates and interval widths.

Taken together, the H2 results do not support the pre-registered prediction that genres differ meaningfully in their association with wellbeing. The pooled heterogeneity estimates fall below the smallest effect size of interest on both the within- and between-person dimensions, genre terms do not improve out-of-sample prediction (Appendix D), and the wide credible intervals for rare genres preclude confident inference about any specific genre–wellbeing pair.

Robustness

Three sensitivity analyses probe the conclusions’ dependence on analytic choices; all three leave every conclusion intact. Adjusting for age, gender, and ethnicity shifts the H1 coefficients by less than 0.01 points and changes no ROPE verdict (Appendix D, Table 5). Halving or doubling the heterogeneity hyperprior scales leaves the H2 parameters essentially unchanged (Appendix D, Table 6). Refitting on multiply imputed data (m = 100) reproduces the H1 equivalence under the pre-registered 90% CI rule (equivalence tests are two one-sided tests at α = .05, which correspond to a 90% rather than a 95% interval; Lakens (2017)) and rejects genre-coefficient equality in neither pooled dimension (Appendix D, Table 8). Full specifications, results, and diagnostics for all three analyses, together with the predictive model comparison and a description of the pre-registered frequentist analysis supplement, are reported in Appendix D.

Exploratory Results: The Daily Timescale

Participants in the analysed daily sample contribute a median of 20 diary days, and participation declines from 1,185 responses on day 1 to 411 on day 30. Windows have a median length of 13.7 hours and close at the survey completion timestamp, so 60.8% of person-days record zero console/PC play in the window. Both positive controls pass in this subsample: self-reported past-24-hour play agrees with telemetry in a matched 24-hour window on 70.7% of responses (φ = 0.39), and men play more Shooter than women (d = 0.27).

Figure 6 displays the posteriors against the ROPE. At the daily level, the within-person association between same-day playtime and life satisfaction was positive, at β = 0.18 points per additional hour in the standalone total-playtime model (M0; 95% CrI [0, 0.35]), with the lower credible bound at zero and the entire posterior inside the ROPE (100%); the multi-membership model’s fixed effect agrees (M3: β = 0.14, 95% CrI [-0.19, 0.42]). The interval widens past zero under two of the three robustness refits (Appendix D). Person-to-person variation in this slope was practically negligible: the random-slope SD was 0.64 (95% CrI [0.18, 0.97]), with 98.3% of the posterior below the SESOI. Between persons, with habitual play measured in full-day hours, participants who play more than others reported slightly lower daily life satisfaction: M0 gives β = -0.43 points per habitual daily hour (95% CrI [-1.11, 0.27]), a negative lean whose posterior sits 95% inside the ROPE; M3 gives β = -0.46 (95% CrI [-1.18, 0.27]); and the all-responses refit, which scores unobserved play as zero, gives β = -0.52 (95% CrI [-1.18, 0.15]) (Table 11).

Genre heterogeneity at the daily level followed the same pattern. Within persons, all three specifications place genre heterogeneity inside the ROPE: the unpooled M1 gives an SD across the 14 genre coefficients of 0.61 (95% CrI [0.39, 0.85]; computed at each posterior draw and noise-inflated, as at the biweekly level, yet with 99.8% of its posterior below the SESOI), the hierarchical prior gives τwithin = 0.15 (95% CrI [0.01, 0.43]; 100% below the SESOI), and the multi-membership model gives σs,within = 0.32 (95% CrI [0.01, 0.98]; 97.7% below the SESOI). The between-person results are inconclusive rather than negligible: τbetween = 0.84 (95% CrI [0.09, 1.86]) straddles the SESOI, with 67.3% of its posterior below it; σs,between = 0.19 (95% CrI [0.01, 0.68]) keeps 99.5% of its posterior below it; and M1’s between-person raw SD (2.37, 95% CrI [1.48, 3.5]) sits far above it, with the usual estimation-error inflation.

Discussion

When previous work has reported that time spent gaming carries no meaningful association with wellbeing, the objection, from skeptics, to parents, to clinicians, and players alike, is that surely it must depend on the type of game one plays. After all, a relaxing puzzle game and a competitive shooter should not plausibly have the same effect on the person playing them. Video game heterogeneity is the standing explanation for why aggregate playtime nulls should not be taken at face value, since a null total association can be produced by heterogeneous true effects that offset one another in aggregate (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025; Yarkoni, 2019). We found this argument persuasive enough to register it as our hypotheses, expecting overall playtime to have no effect on wellbeing, but for genres to differ. This this study was built to answer that question.

The question has stood open for at least three decades, since Griffiths (1993) reviewed the evidence on ‘computer games’, not for lack of interest but for lack of measurement. Many awnsers have been proposed (ref) and refuted (ref), it has even impacted policy decisions and public opinion (refs needed). However, all prior genre research carried at least one of three limitations, and usually more than one at once. First, genre assignment is often subjective, roughly half of the genre studies employ a bespoke classification, one in five never state the basis of its categories, and labels are typically self-assigned by participants or researchers, meaning the same games are habitually classified into different genres across studies (Starosta et al., 2024). Second, playtime has often been self-reported rather than logged, and self-reported and logged playtime correlate positively but far from perfectly (our own positive control puts the biweekly correlation at r = 0.469) (ref ellis). Third, Research designs often cover a single game or a handful of titles (Brühlmann et al., 2020; Johannes et al., 2021; Larrieu et al., 2023), leaving genre contrasts to be assembled across different studies that classified and measured both play and genre incommensurably, instead of one study with a single ground truth. This study clears all three obstacles at once. Measuring objective session-level telemetry across Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam;uutelising one crowd-sourced genre taxonomy applied uniformly to 94.1% of in-study play, estimating 14 genres jointly in one sample with models capable of analysing games carrying multiple genre labels.making it, to our knowledge, the first study positioned to answer the questions directly.

The playtime-wellbeing association is practically equivalent to zero

Does playtime in general have an effect on wellbeing? H1 predicted not, and both components of the hypothesis were supported (see Figure 3 and Table 10). Within persons, when participants played more than their own average in a given two-week wave, their wellbeing barely changed, consistent with previous digital trace studies that have repeatedly found aggregate playtime to be a poor predictor of wellbeing fluctuations (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024; Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025; Larrieu et al., 2023). Between persons, practical equivalence was likewise established.

Inverting these estimates makes their practical magnitude concrete. The determined SESOI derives from the smallest wellbeing change a person can themselves notice (Ballou, Sewall, et al., 2024; Maheswaran et al., 2012), divided by the roughly 5 hours of daily leisure realistically available for reallocation (Sturm & Cohen, 2019). Against that anchor, the estimates are not merely small; the doses they imply are unreachable. For wellbeing to shift by one minimally important difference, the within-person point estimate requires roughly 98 additional hours of play per day, several times more hours than a day contains, and even the credible bound most favourable to an effect requires 22 extra daily hours, more extreme than the 10 additional daily hours that Vuorre & Przybylski (2022) derived from game-level telemetry. These doses are so small the even the sample’s variation cannot contain them: of the 1,500 participants observed across adjacent waves, only 121 ever changed their average daily play by 4 or more hours from one wave to the next, and the largest swing recorded anywhere in the sample was 9.3 hours per day. And if a player reallocated the entire 5-hour daily leisure budget into or out of gaming, the implied shift of about 0.015 points would still sit far below the roughly 0.2 points of measurement error that surround an individual’s score on the parent WEMWBS [1 SEM; Maheswaran et al. (2012)]. An association that no achievable dose can reach and that its own instrument cannot accurately measure is, for every practical purpose, indistinguishable from no association at all.

Genres do not matter for the playtime-wellbeing association

We expected genres to differ in how playtime relates to fluctuations in general mental wellbeing, however the findings disconfirmed our registered hypothesis. The point estimates of genre-to-genre variation in the within-person per-hour association fell at or below the smallest effect we deemed practically meaningful in all three model specifications; the 14 within-person genre estimates span only -0.018 to +0.013 under the hierarchical prior, with no estimate more than a third of the SESOI from zero, and the most-played genres by total playtime (Role Playing Game (RPG), Adventure, Strategy, Shooter; see Figure 1) sit inside this same narrow band. The complete-case joint test does detect a departure from exact within-person coefficient equality, but of a magnitude well below the SESOI (Appendix D). Meaning that, genres proved statistically distinguishable but practically interchangeable. One noticible exception is M3’s σs, which retains roughly a fifth of its posterior mass above the SESOI, so within-person heterogeneity slightly beyond the threshold cannot be fully excluded. Thus, the effect of seperate genres canceling out a general playtime effect is below the threshold of noticeability, and any defence of playtime nulls that appeals to the heterogeneous nature of video games must look to partitions finer than genre.

Who Plays, Not What Playing Does

The contrast between light and heavy players is a different quantity from either hypothesis test. Participants who habitually play more reported slightly lower average wellbeing, however the same participants’ wellbeing did not fall in waves when they played more than usual. This effect is small in practical terms, two otherwise-similar people would need to differ by between roughly 9 hours of habitual daily play (at the credible bound most favourable to an effect) and 18 hours (at the point estimate), in either case more than the roughly 5 hours of daily leisure available, before their expected wellbeing differed noticeably. Its interpretation matters more than its size. That within-null / between-negative pattern is a potential selection effect, people with lower baseline wellbeing spending more time in games rather than games lowering wellbeing, though a cumulative effect accruing over years would look the same at these timescales (cf. Vuorre & Przybylski, 2022); it recurs across observational media research (Ballou, Vuorre, et al., 2025; Kievit et al., 2013; Robinson, 1950; Rohrer & Murayama, 2023). The genre-level results carry the same finging. Descriptively, the largest positive between-person point estimate belongs to Sport (0.022, 95% CrI [-0.011, 0.08] in M2), yet its within-person counterpart is null (-0.006, 95% CrI [-0.034, 0.016]): people who favour sport games may, for example, be more physically or socially active, rather than playing the sport genre itself improving wellbeing, consistent with exploratory work concluding that players select the games that align with their personal sources of enjoyment (Griffith & Sharpe, 2024). The best available causal evidence points in the opposite direction, console-lottery estimates from Egami et al. (2024) are positive, 0.1 to 0.6 standard deviations, on data whose own observational analysis correlates negatively. Our within-person null estimates, which remove stable person-level confounding, demonstarte that public claims about gamers’ mental health are, in effect, reports about who plays, not about what playing does.

Individual Susceptibility Is Bounded at These Timescales

Still, a null average could conceal a minority for whom play genuinely matters (cf. Karhulahti et al., 2025). The random slope in M0 addresses this directly by modelling every participant’s own within-person association between playtime and wellbeing. The standard deviation of these person-specific slopes describes how much people differ from the average. That standard deviation was 0.035 (95% CrI: [0.005, 0.062]), with only 3.8% of its posterior above the SESOI. Individuals in the far tails of that distribution may still exceed the SESOI, but we would argue that they are the exception the spread allows rather than a subgroup the data reveal. Two boundaries on this claim are required. These are bounds on general wellbeing at biweekly resolution and on life satisfaction at daily resolution, among adults screened into the study at ages 18 to 40; they say nothing about disordered play, where genre-linked structural characteristics remain plausibly relevant (André et al., 2024; Rehbein et al., 2021), and nothing about children. Future work should address these questions.

Shortening the Window Does Not Recover an Effect

Lastly, a final possible objection is temporal, namely that the wellbeing effects of play might surface and dissipate faster than a biweekly retrospective survey can register. To test this claim, the exploratory daily analysis shortens the window from fourteen days to one and reproduces both conclusions. Within persons, every estimate lies inside the equivalence region under every specification, and the same-day point estimate is positive, roughly double its biweekly counterpart in within-person standard-deviation units (0.014 versus 0.009 sw per hour). The direction is consistent with the session-level affective uplift reported among PowerWash Simulator players (Vuorre et al., 2024) and with the positive causal estimates of Egami et al. (2024), though its resolution is fragile across the robustness refits and should be read as suggestive rather than resolved. Its practical magnitude is negligible either way: shifting daily life satisfaction by one minimally important difference (5 points) would require 28 additional hours of same-day play, more hours than a day contains, and within-person genre heterogeneity at the daily level is likewise bounded (its between-person counterpart is inconclusive rather than negligible). Therefore,moving the measurement closer in time, on its own, does not conjure a meaningfull effect.

Are all games the same?

The question this study set out to answer rests on an intuition, that games differ psychologically, and although genre labels are not the way to find that difference, the intuition survives the answer. What fails is its operationalisation. Game scholars have argued for decades that genre labels are conventions of marketing and library organisation rather than coherent descriptions of play: they conflate gameplay style, purpose, and mood in a single word (Lee et al., 2014), fail elementary classificatory tests (Clarke et al., 2017), and drift as the medium evolves (Cohen, 1986; Vargas-Iglesias, 2020). The public, policymakers, and psychological reseachers, imported the labels anyway, and the present results show what they are worth as a predictor of wellbeing. This study has provided the fairest test possible to find genre-specific effect, and found that genre carries no meaningfull effect. The pathways plausibly connecting play to wellbeing seem to operate at levels that genre labels cannot index (Ballou, Hakman, et al., 2025): need satisfaction depends on autonomy-supportive design features (Ballou et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2012), social capital depends on co-play relationships (Depping et al., 2018; Vella et al., 2015), and affect regulation depends on the match between gameplay and current emotional state (Kosa et al., 2020). Dedicated taxonomies of structural game features now exist for characterising these directly (Saini & Hodgins, 2023). And within a single game, behavioural variation in how people play is associated with meaningful wellbeing differences while genre is held constant (Hakman et al., 2026). If wellbeing differs among people playing the same game, a label that treats those people as identical is potentially measuring the wrong thing. The person who objects that a puzzle game and a shooter cannot do the same thing is right that the games differ; but the effect of playing them on wellbeing does not.

Policy implications

For public guidance, the implication is uncomfortable because hours are the quantity institutions know how to handle, time is the property of play most readily measured, displayed, and limited, and it is where wellbeing guidance therefore concentrates (ref the screentime bans). Our estimates predict what such instruments can deliver on the margin they operate on, hours among people already playing, if the observed association were causal, shifting daily play by a full hour, in either direction and sustained for weeks, would move wellbeing by an unnoticeable and irrelevent amount. Steering adults between genres is similarly unpromising, the heterogeneity estimates describe freely chosen play, and reassigning players to genres they would not choose is a different intervention, one these data cannot speak to. If the aim is wellbeing, playtime is the wrong lever. Read in the other direction the same results are actually reassuring. Within the range of ordinary adult play we observed, no specification provides positive evidence of a practically meaningful wellbeing cost for any genre, though intervals for rarely played genres remain wide, popular worries about particular genres receive no support at these margins.

Methodolocial Contribution:A Model for Overlapping Categories

Methodologically, the multi-membership model transfers beyond games. To our knowledge this is the first application in media psychology of the model class, developed originally for educational data where students attend multiple schools (Cafri et al., 2015; Fielding & Goldstein, 2006). It treats a game’s genres the way the data present them, as overlapping memberships with composition weights, rather than forcing single-category assignment or independent fixed effects. Partial pooling through σs stabilises sparse categories, and the specification was validated by parameter recovery before touching real data. Any media effects question with overlapping content labels has the same structure (e.g.,streaming titles with multiple genre tags, news diets spanning outlets with overlapping orientations, social media feeds spanning topic categories) and can be answered with the same model. The code was open-sourced and made freely available to support future applications of this method.

Limitations

Several limitations constrain these conclusions and point at the work that should come next. First, the design is observational, the within-person decomposition removes stable confounds but not time-varying ones (life events, seasons), and our causal statements are correspondingly guarded (Rohrer & Murayama, 2023). Second, the SWEMWBS is a global instrument assessed over a two-week recall window, gaming competes with sleep, work, and social life for within-person wellbeing variance, and domain-specific outcomes (affect, sleep, connectedness) could show associations a global measure averages away. The daily analysis takes the first step down this temporal hierarchy and still finds nothing of practical size, which only sharpens rather than settles the point. Future work should pair session-level telemetry with momentary assessment, and use time-use data to partial gaming from competing activities. Third, coverage is imperfect, the achieved platform-coverage criterion admitted participants with as little as half of their play observed, mobile play carries no genre metadata, and in-study minutes are dominated by Steam (84.1%, versus 12.8% Xbox and 3.1% Nintendo), so the genre findings are predominantly findings about PC play by UK and US adults. Fourth, rare genres were estimated imprecisely, their effecs remain untested rather than refuted, a data sparsity problem that larger samples or finer temporal resolution could solve.

Appendix A: Genre Mapping

Genre labels from all three platforms resolve to the study taxonomy in two steps: Xbox store labels are first mapped onto IGDB genres (per the pre-registration’s Appendix B), and raw IGDB labels (23 distinct labels observed in the study metadata) are then collapsed into 14 analysis-level categories. Table 2 presents both steps in one place: each row is an implemented study genre, with the raw IGDB labels it subsumes, the Xbox store labels routed to it, and, where the pre-registered mapping (which would yield 17 distinct genres on the observed labels) treated a label differently, the pre-registered assignment. The implemented mapping diverges from the pre-registered one in both directions: it preserves granularity for sub-genres that prior literature treats as distinct (Hack-and-slash/Beat-’em-up, Point-and-click, Visual Novel), collapses more aggressively elsewhere (MOBA into Strategy, Card & Board Game into Puzzle, Pinball and Music into Arcade), and excludes Indie as a non-substantive label (see Appendix B, Deviation D2). Two details sit outside the table: the Xbox label Family + Kids has no IGDB equivalent and is resolved by the title’s secondary genre, and IGDB includes no top-level “Action” category, so what is colloquially called “action” is distributed across Shooter, Hack-and-slash, Fighting, and Platform.

Appendix B: Deviations from Pre-Registration

This appendix documents all known deviations from the Stage 1 pre-registration (Ballou, Földes, et al., 2024) in a single numbered scheme (D1–D9). Every deviation is presented in the structured disclosure format of Willroth and Atherton (2024), reporting the type of deviation, the original pre-registered wording, a description of what was done instead, the reason, the timing relative to data access and results, and the potential impact on interpretation. Related decisions are documented together rather than split across entries: prior specification is part of the inference-framework deviation (D4), the H2 model-structure decisions form a single deviation (D5), and the three changes that arose upstream during data collection (outside the authors’ control and reported in full by Ballou, Földes, et al. (2025)) are consolidated as D9. One unregistered correction, which implements the pre-registered plan more faithfully than the upstream data pipeline did, is documented last in the same format (U1).

D2 Genre taxonomy (sub-genre collapsing) Data preparation After data access, before results known
