Structured disclosures

D1: Genre assignment (full attribution)

Field Content
Type Data preparation
Original wording Games are classified by their primary (first) IGDB genre. The pre-registration does not specify how to handle multi-genre games beyond this.
Deviation description Each game’s full playtime is attributed to every one of its IGDB genre labels (all labels retained; up to 16 raw labels per game observed in the metadata). A game with 2 hours of play and two genre labels (e.g., Adventure + RPG) contributes 2 hours to each genre. Genre hours therefore represent total exposure to games carrying that label and are not mutually exclusive: summing across genres exceeds total playtime. Total playtime for H1 is computed separately from raw sessions without genre duplication. An earlier draft capped attribution at 3 genres per game; the cap was removed because 25% of games with any genre label carry more than 3 raw IGDB labels and truncation discards classification information.
Reason Many games genuinely span multiple genres; restricting to the primary genre discards meaningful classification information and introduces arbitrary dependence on IGDB’s label ordering. Full attribution reflects actual exposure to each genre.
Timing After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known
Reader impact Full attribution means genre-level playtime variables cannot be summed to recover total playtime, and each genre coefficient estimates the association with exposure to games carrying that label rather than the effect of the genre in isolation. This is appropriate because a player of an Adventure-RPG is fully exposed to both Adventure and RPG design elements. Total playtime is tracked independently to avoid conflating genre exposure with total gaming time. The pre-registered primary-genre analysis is reported in the supplement.

D2: Genre taxonomy (sub-genre collapsing)

Field Content
Type Data preparation
Original wording The pre-registration collapses IGDB sub-genres as follows: Hack and slash/Beat ’em up → Action; Point-and-click and Visual Novel → Adventure; Turn-based strategy, Real-time strategy, and Tactical → Strategy; Quiz/Trivia → Puzzle.
Deviation description Hack-and-slash/Beat-’em-up, Point-and-click, and Visual Novel are retained as distinct categories; MOBA is folded into Strategy; Card & Board Game joins Quiz/Trivia under Puzzle; Pinball and Music are folded into Arcade; Indie is excluded as a non-substantive label. The implemented taxonomy comprises 14 analysis-level categories (full mapping in Appendix A of this manuscript). The metadata contain 23 distinct raw IGDB labels; the pre-registration’s body text mentions 19 IGDB genres while its own Appendix A lists all 23, and we report the count as observed in the data.
Reason The pre-registered collapsing conflated meaningfully different genres; e.g., Visual Novels and Beat-’em-ups would both disappear into broad categories despite prior literature treating them as psychologically distinct. Retaining them preserves granularity where theory suggests it matters.
Timing After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known
Reader impact Genre-level coefficients refer to different category boundaries than the pre-registration implies, so per-genre estimates are not directly comparable to a hypothetical analysis under the original taxonomy. The retained sub-genres are rarely played, producing wide credible intervals for those categories; the pooled heterogeneity parameters (M2, M3) are designed to remain stable under this sparsity.

D3: Telemetry–survey alignment

Field Content
Type Variables
Original wording Not specified; the pre-registration implicitly assumes wave windows counted forward from the baseline day (days 0–83).
Deviation description Playtime windows are aligned retrospectively to the survey: each wave’s playtime covers the 14 days ending the day before the biweekly survey, so wave 1 covers days −14 to −1 relative to baseline. Pre-baseline telemetry is available for all three platforms because participants linked their accounts at intake.
Reason SWEMWBS asks participants to reflect on “the past 2 weeks.” The wave 1 survey is completed on the baseline day, so its retrospective window predates the study start; forward-counted windows would misalign every wave’s playtime with the period participants were actually reporting on.
Timing After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known
Reader impact Improves measurement validity by matching exposure and outcome windows. Estimates are not directly comparable to an analysis using forward-counted windows, and wave 1 relies on telemetry recorded before the study formally began (over 85% of participants per platform had observable telemetry covering the full wave 1 period).

D4: Inference framework and priors (frequentist → Bayesian)

Field Content
Type Inferential criteria
Original wording H1 will be tested via equivalence test with SESOI = ±0.06 SWEMWBS points per 1-hour change in daily playtime, using 90% CIs (TOST procedure). H2 will be tested via a joint Wald test via car::linearHypothesis(). The pre-registration specifies no priors (all models frequentist).
Deviation description Both H1 and H2 are estimated using Bayesian multilevel models [brms; Bürkner (2017)] rather than frequentist lmer. H1 is evaluated via ROPE analysis with bounds identical to the pre-registered SESOI [−0.06, +0.06]; if >95% of the posterior falls within the ROPE, practical equivalence is established (Kruschke, 2018). H2 is evaluated through posterior genre-heterogeneity parameters (\sigma_s in M3, \tau in M2, the SD of coefficients in M1), with magnitude judged against the SESOI. Because the pre-registration specifies no priors, these were chosen as weakly informative on the 1–5 item-mean outcome scale: Student-t(3, 0, 0.5) on fixed-effect coefficients, Student-t(3, 3, 2) on the intercept, Half-Normal(0, 0.1) on M2’s \tau hyperparameters, Half-Normal(0, 0.3) on M3’s \sigma_s (looser to accommodate the more challenging multi-membership posterior geometry), and brms defaults on remaining variance components. The pre-registered frequentist models (TOST and joint Wald tests) are reported in full in the pre-registered analysis supplement.
Reason A Bayesian framework provides richer equivalence testing via ROPE and continuous uncertainty quantification; the priors regularise estimation without strongly constraining the posterior.
Timing After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known
Reader impact The SESOI is unchanged and the ROPE procedure provides a continuous measure of practical equivalence rather than a binary significance decision. Risk of bias is low: the equivalence region is identical and the deviation was decided before results were known. More diffuse priors could permit larger heterogeneity estimates; prior sensitivity could be assessed by varying the prior scales.

D5: H2 model specifications

Field Content
Type Analytic approach
Original wording H2 uses genre-specific fixed-effect coefficients with a random intercept and uncorrelated random slopes for all within-person genre predictors (zero-correlation syntax), tested via a joint Wald test. The pre-registration anticipates identifiability issues and specifies dropping random slopes if the model is singular.
Deviation description Three related decisions. (a) The pre-registered random slopes (14 genres × 2 dimensions = 28 slope parameters) render the model near-singular; the random-intercept-only contingency was applied, as pre-registered. (b) Two additional specifications were added: M2 replaces the independent priors on genre coefficients with a learned hierarchical prior (\tau), and M3 is a multi-membership random-effects model in which genre modulates the total playtime slope via composition weights, adopted as the primary H2 analysis. (c) For M3, each wave’s membership weights are that wave’s genre shares of total genre-attributed playtime; waves with zero playtime receive uniform weights (1/K), a technical requirement of brms::mm().
Reason With 28 independently estimated genre coefficients, the pre-registered specification is overparameterised and rare-genre estimates are dominated by sampling noise. The pooled specifications (M2, M3) separate genuine genre heterogeneity from estimation error and answer H2 through a single interpretable parameter.
Timing The random-slope contingency was applied at model fitting. M2 and M3 were added after the fixed-effects (M1) results were known.
Reader impact The timing of adding M2 and M3 (after seeing M1 results) increases risk of bias for the choice of primary analysis; readers who prefer the pre-registered specification can rely on the M1 results, reported in full, which lead to the same qualitative conclusion. The M3 specification was validated with a parameter-recovery simulation before being fit to real data. Uniform weights for zero-playtime waves have minimal substantive impact, as those observations contribute little information to genre-specific estimates.

D6: H1 platform scope (mobile excluded)

Field Content
Type Variables
Original wording H1 will test the association between total cross-platform playtime and wellbeing, using data from all five platforms (Nintendo, Xbox, Steam, iOS, Android).
Deviation description H1 total playtime is computed from Nintendo, Xbox, and Steam only, excluding iOS and Android. Mobile platforms provide only daily aggregate minutes without game-level data (D9). Including mobile for H1 but not H2 would mean “total playtime” refers to different quantities across hypotheses.
Reason Internal consistency between H1 and H2.
Timing After data access, before results of the pre-registered approach were known
Reader impact This reduces the total playtime measure by excluding mobile gaming. However, mobile contributed a small minority of total playtime for most participants. The pre-registered analysis supplement retains the all-platform total, allowing a direct comparison of console/PC-only versus all-platform H1 estimates. Risk of bias is low: the deviation was motivated by internal consistency, not by the data or results.

D7: Outcome measure and scoring

Field Content
Type Variables
Original wording General mental wellbeing will be measured with the WEMWBS (Tennant et al., 2007).
Deviation description The instrument administered in the Open Play study is the short-form SWEMWBS (7 items, each scored 1–5), an upstream design decision documented by Ballou, Földes, et al. (2025). The score is computed as the item mean (rowMeans of the 7 items, range 1–5), not the summed score (range 7–35). The pre-registered SESOI of 0.06 per hour/day was derived by Ballou, Sewall, et al. (2024) on the 1–5 item-mean scale (0.3 minimally important difference ÷ 5 hours of realistic daily leisure), and the pre-registration’s own precision analysis assumes a within-person SD of 0.7, which is only coherent on the 1–5 scale. An earlier version of this analysis used rowSums, which inflated coefficients by a factor of 7 relative to the scale the SESOI was defined on.
Reason Item-mean scoring places the coefficients, priors, and SESOI on a single consistent scale.
Timing Instrument: during data collection, before data access (upstream). Scoring: after data access, before results were known.
Reader impact No change to the underlying data or model specification; only the summary score computation differs from a summed-score reading of the pre-registration. All downstream numbers (coefficients, equivalence tests, ROPE bounds) are on the scale the SESOI was designed for.

D8: Missing data handling

Field Content
Type Analytic approach
Original wording Missing data: multiple imputation via mice package (predictive mean matching, wide format). Report both complete-case and imputed results.
Deviation description Outcome missingness has two components. Among submitted surveys, 43 responses (0.6% of 6,723 in the analytic sample) are missing SWEMWBS, all with every item missing. The larger component is wave nonresponse: 4,348 of 11,028 person-waves (39.4%) in the analytic sample were never submitted (response declined from 100% at wave 1 to 40% at wave 6). Instead of the pre-registered single-level wide-format PMM, we imputed on the complete participant × wave grid with hierarchical two-level MICE (2l.pmm, participants as clusters, ±1-wave lag/lead terms, fully observed exposures with explicit person means, intake auxiliaries), the protocol shared with the programmatic RR’s other Stage 2 outputs; the number of imputations follows von Hippel’s (2020) rule from the pilot fraction of missing information. The primary Bayesian models remain fit to observed outcomes (valid under MAR given the modelled covariates and random effects); pooled frequentist counterparts on the imputed data are reported in Appendix D. The imputation grid covers the analytic sample; 110 surveyed participants with no valid SWEMWBS in any wave provide no outcome information to anchor imputation and are outside both the analytic sample and the grid.
Reason The pre-registered wide-format single-level PMM understates the hierarchical structure, and an initial implementation of it could only address item-level missingness among submitted surveys. The grid protocol addresses the dominant wave-nonresponse component and is consistent with the sibling Stage 2 studies.
Timing Complete-case-first decision: after data access, before results known. Grid-imputation protocol: adopted after complete-case results were known, by mirroring the sibling studies’ protocol rather than tailoring choices to results.
Reader impact The imputation model conditions on all analysis-model exposures, so it is congenial with (indeed richer than) the analysis models. Equivalence and joint-test conclusions are unchanged under imputation (see Sensitivity Analyses); the pooled between-person interval widens because person means are genuinely uncertain for participants with few observed waves (high fraction of missing information), which Rubin’s rules propagate. If nonresponse depends on unobserved wellbeing beyond the modelled covariates (MNAR), both complete-case and imputed estimates could be biased in the same direction; the agreement between them rules out bias from the modelled missingness mechanism, not MNAR.

D9: Upstream data-collection changes

Field Content
Type Data collection procedures
Original wording Age range 18–75 (UK) and 18–30 (US); ≥75% of gaming time on included platforms; Android telemetry collected as session-level exports via ActivityWatch.
Deviation description Three changes made by the Open Play team during data collection, before this study’s data access: (a) screening admitted ages 18–40 in both regions; (b) the platform coverage threshold was lowered to ≥50%; (c) Android data were collected as daily aggregate minutes via Digital Wellbeing screenshots rather than session-level exports. All three are reported in full by Ballou, Földes, et al. (2025).
Reason Recruitment and data-collection constraints in the upstream Open Play study; outside the authors’ control.
Timing During data collection, before data access
Reader impact The narrower age range limits generalisability to older adults. The lower coverage threshold admits participants with a larger share of unobserved play, adding measurement error to total playtime. The Android granularity change restricts Android to daily totals, contributing to the pre-registered all-platform sensitivity analysis only and excluding it from H2 (see D6).

Unregistered correction

U1: Xbox genre mapping correction

Field Content
Type Data preparation (correction, consistent with the pre-registration)
Original wording Xbox genres are mapped onto the IGDB taxonomy via the mapping table in the pre-registration’s Appendix B.
Deviation description The upstream Open Play preprocessing pipeline (label_genres.R) failed to map approximately 67% of Xbox playtime to IGDB genres due to a string-formatting bug (exact-match against multi-value and inconsistently-formatted genre strings). We applied a corrected mapping in our preprocessing using the xbox_primary_genre and xbox_subgenre metadata fields, recovering genre information for an additional 20.7 million minutes of Xbox playtime. This is a fix, not a deviation: the pre-registration explicitly specified the Xbox-to-IGDB mapping, and the correction implements it as intended.
Reason Implementing the pre-registered mapping faithfully; the upstream bug would otherwise cause systematic genre-data missingness for the largest platform by volume.
Timing After data access, before results were known
Reader impact Xbox genre coverage increased from 33% to 80% of playtime, substantially reducing systematic missingness in the genre-level analyses.

Appendix D: Sensitivity and Supplementary Analyses

This appendix reports the three sensitivity analyses summarised under Robustness in the main text: demographic covariate adjustment, hyperprior-scale sensitivity for the genre heterogeneity parameters, and multiple imputation of wave nonresponse (with distributional diagnostics). It then reports the predictive model comparison (whether genre terms improve out-of-sample prediction), followed by a description of the pre-registered frequentist analysis supplement.

Demographic Covariates

The pre-registration specified a sensitivity analysis adjusting the primary models for demographic covariates. We refit M0 (total playtime) and M1 (genre fixed effects) with age, gender, and ethnicity added as population-level predictors, using the subset of participants with complete demographic data.

The adjusted models use 6,464 observations from 1,694 participants with complete demographic data. Table 5 compares the primary and covariate-adjusted estimates. The H1 coefficients shift by at most 0.007 points after adjustment, and the ROPE conclusions are unchanged: 100% of the adjusted within-person posterior falls inside the ROPE (primary: 100%), and 100% of the adjusted between-person posterior (primary: 100%). One qualification: the adjusted between-person credible interval ([-0.041, -0.006]) excludes zero, unlike the unadjusted interval; this small negative association remains far inside the ROPE and is consistent with the selection account discussed under H1. The genre heterogeneity estimates are likewise essentially unaffected. Both adjusted models converged cleanly (max R-hat = 1.008, 0 divergent transitions). Demographic composition therefore does not account for the observed associations.

Prior Sensitivity

The heterogeneity hyperpriors are the component of the specification where prior choice could most plausibly shape the H2 conclusion, since the Half-Normal(0, 0.1) prior on M2’s τ places its own median near the SESOI. As committed to in Deviation D4, we therefore refit M2 with the hyperprior scale halved and doubled (0.05, 0.20) and M3 with its σs scale halved and doubled (0.15, 0.60), using otherwise identical specifications (R/03_prior_sensitivity.R).

Table 6 shows that the heterogeneity conclusions are not an artefact of the hyperprior scales. Both parameters are essentially unchanged when their hyperprior scales are halved or doubled: M2’s τ estimates agree to the third decimal across the fourfold range of scales, and M3’s σs posterior median and its posterior mass below the SESOI shift only trivially. This is consistent with both posteriors being strongly data-dominated (the posterior SDs are roughly a tenth of the corresponding prior SDs). Across all specifications and scales, the qualitative conclusion is the same as in the main analysis: genre heterogeneity at or below the smallest effect size of interest.

Multiple Imputation

The pre-registration specified multiple imputation by chained equations with predictive mean matching. We implemented the two-level grid protocol described in Methods (Missing Data): across the 11,028-cell participant × wave grid, 4,348 cells (39.4%) had no observed SWEMWBS (Table 7), and m = 100 imputed datasets were generated. The pilot fractions of missing information for the H1 coefficients were 0.57 (within-person) and 0.91 (between-person): the between-person coefficient depends on person means that are genuinely uncertain for participants with few observed waves, and Rubin’s rules propagate that uncertainty into the pooled intervals. Von Hippel’s rule would require 167 imputations for a 5%-stable standard error; with m = 100 the achieved coefficient of variation of the pooled standard errors is approximately 0.06, which widens the pooled intervals slightly but does not affect the equivalence verdicts.

Table 8 compares complete-case and pooled imputed results. The H1 conclusions are unchanged: both pooled 90% confidence intervals fall entirely within the pre-registered equivalence bounds of ±0.06, so practical equivalence holds on the imputed data. The between-person interval widens under imputation, reflecting that person-mean wellbeing is uncertain for participants with few observed waves.

For H2, the comparison surfaces the distinction between statistical and practical significance that motivates the SESOI. On the complete cases, the joint Wald test rejects exact equality of the 14 within-person genre coefficients (χ²(13) = 25.0, p = 0.023); under the pre-registered decision rule this reading is limited to “at least one pair of genres differs”, with no pairwise interpretation absent formal post-hoc tests. The magnitude of that departure is the quantity the SESOI governs, and it is small: the SD of the 14 coefficient estimates is 0.022 (complete-case) and 0.025 (imputed), both well below 0.06 and consistent with M1’s posterior heterogeneity estimate. On the imputed data the pooled D_1 tests reject neither dimension (within: p = 0.847; between: p = 0.454), though these tests carry reduced power at this level of missing information (relative increase in variance 0.54 for the within-person constraints). The between-person joint test rejects in neither frame. Distributional diagnostics for the imputation are reported in Appendix D (Figure 7). In sum, accounting for wave nonresponse leaves every conclusion intact: total playtime is practically equivalent to zero, and genre heterogeneity, statistically detectable or not depending on the frame, remains below the smallest effect size of interest.

Distributional Diagnostics

The central plausibility check for the imputation model is distributional: imputed wellbeing values should occupy the same range as the observed data and differ from it only in ways explicable by which participants are missing, not by model artefacts.

Figure 7 shows the imputed values to be distributionally almost indistinguishable from the observed data: pooled across all 100 imputations, the imputed values have mean 0.009 and SD 0.74 on the centred scale, against an observed mean of 0 (by construction) and SD of 0.75. The imputation model neither compresses the outcome’s variance nor shifts nonresponders’ imputed wellbeing to implausible regions of the scale. Convergence traces and strip plots are produced alongside the cached imputation (output/qc_imputation/).

Predictive Model Comparison

A complementary way to ask whether genre matters is through predictive performance: does adding genre-specific terms to the total-playtime-only M0 baseline improve out-of-sample prediction? We assess this using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) via Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (Vehtari et al., 2017). A positive difference in expected log predictive density (ELPD) relative to M0 indicates that genre terms help.

M0, the model with total playtime only, showed the highest expected log predictive density, and all three genre specifications predicted slightly worse out-of-sample (Table 9), with ELPD deficits between one and roughly two standard errors of the difference. Adding genre information, in any of the three specifications, therefore does not improve the prediction of wellbeing over total playtime alone. Pareto-k diagnostics flagged 5.2–5.5% of observations per model (k > 0.7; 349–368 observations), so the ELPD values are approximate; this affects the precision of the differences, not the ordering. The inferential reach of this comparison is considered in the Discussion.

Pre-Registered Frequentist Analysis

The full pre-registered analysis (primary-genre attribution, frequentist within-between models fit with lmer, TOST equivalence tests for H1, joint Wald tests for H2, and multiple imputation via mice alongside complete-case results) is reported in the supplementary materials as a standalone document. It also retains the pre-registered all-platform total playtime measure (including iOS and Android; Appendix B, Deviation D6), providing the comparison between console/PC-only and all-platform H1 estimates.

Daily-Timescale Sensitivity Analyses

Four sensitivity refits accompany the exploratory daily analysis (see Exploratory Daily-Timescale Analysis in Methods). Allowing first-order autocorrelated residuals with a within-person day trend (estimated AR(1) = 0.31) widens the within-person interval past zero (β = 0.14, 95% CrI [-0.02, 0.29]), as does adjusting for window length (β = 0.15, 95% CrI [-0.03, 0.32]). Excluding the 8% of Xbox sessions recorded with date-only timestamps, whose start times are floored to midnight and whose minutes are spread uniformly over the recorded day, leaves the within-person interval above zero (β = 0.18, 95% CrI [0.01, 0.35]). The all-responses refit, which retains every diary response and scores unobserved play as zero, gives the same between-person lean as the analysed sample (β = -0.52, 95% CrI [-1.18, 0.15]). Two qualifications apply to the daily genre-level intervals: they inherit the exchangeable-residual assumption that the autocorrelation refit relaxes for the total-playtime model only, and the hierarchical-prior model’s 18 divergent transitions followed a documented step-size escalation, with estimates stable across both settings.
